L22:       * cite18†Pyodide, Emscripten, and PyScript L23:       * cite19†PyOpenSSL L24:       * cite20†SOCKS Proxies L25:   * cite21†Contributing L26:   * cite22†Security Policy L27:   * cite23†Changelog L28:   * cite24†v2 Migration Guide L29: cite7†Back to top L30: # Advanced Usagecite25†¶ L31: ## Customizing Pool Behaviorcite26†¶ L32: 
L33: The cite27†`PoolManager` class automatically handles creating cite28†`ConnectionPool` instances for each host as needed. By default, it will keep a maximum of 10 cite28†`ConnectionPool` instances. If you’re making requests to many different hosts it might improve performance to increase this number.
L34: 
L35:     import urllib3
L36: 
L37:     http = urllib3.PoolManager(num_pools=50)
L38: 
L39: 
L40: However, keep in mind that this does increase memory and socket consumption.
L41: Similarly, the cite28†`ConnectionPool` class keeps a pool of individual cite29†`HTTPConnection` instances. These connections are used during an individual request and returned to the pool when the request is complete. By default only one connection will be saved for re-use. If you are making many requests to the same host simultaneously it might improve performance to increase this number.
L42: 
L43:     import urllib3
L44: 
L45:     http = urllib3.PoolManager(maxsize=10)
L46:     # Alternatively
L47:     pool = urllib3.HTTPConnectionPool("google.com", maxsize=10)
L48: The behavior of the pooling for cite28†`ConnectionPool` is different from cite27†`PoolManager` . By default, if a new request is made and there is no free connection in the pool then a new connection will be created. However, this connection will not be saved if more than `maxsize` connections exist. This means that `maxsize` does not determine the maximum number of connections that can be open to a particular host, just the maximum number of connections to keep in the pool.
L49: However, if you specify `block=True` then there can be at most `maxsize` connections open to a particular host.
L50: 
L51:     http = urllib3.PoolManager(maxsize=10, block=True)
L52: 
L53:     # Alternatively
L54:     pool = urllib3.HTTPConnectionPool("google.com", maxsize=10, block=True)
L55: Any new requests will block until a connection is available from the pool. This is a great way to prevent flooding a host with too many connections in multi-threaded applications.
L56: ## Streaming and I/Ocite30†¶ L57: 
L58: When using `preload_content=True` (the default setting) the response body will be read immediately into memory and the HTTP connection will be released back into the pool without manual intervention.
L59: 
L60: However, when dealing with responses of large or unknown length, it’s often better to stream the response content using `preload_content=False`. Setting `preload_content` to `False` means that urllib3 will only read from the socket when data is requested.
L61: 
L62: Note
L63: When using `preload_content=False`, you need to manually release the HTTP connection back to the connection pool so that it can be re-used. To ensure the HTTP connection is in a valid state before being re-used all data should be read off the wire.
L64: 
L65: You can call the cite31†`drain_conn()` to throw away unread data still on the wire. This call isn’t necessary if data has already been completely read from the response.
L66: After all data is read you can call cite32†`release_conn()` to release the connection into the pool.
L67: 
L68: You can call the cite33†`close()` to close the connection, but this call doesn’t return the connection to the pool, throws away the unread data on the wire, and leaves the connection in an undefined protocol state. This is desirable if you prefer not reading data from the socket to re-using the HTTP connection.
L69: cite34†`stream()` lets you iterate over chunks of the response content.
L70: 
L71:     import urllib3
L72: 
L73:     resp = urllib3.request(
L74:         "GET",
L75:         "https://httpbin.org/bytes/1024",
L76:         preload_content=False
L77:     )
L78: 
L79:     for chunk in resp.stream(32):
L80:         print(chunk)
L81:         # b"\x9e\xa97'\x8e\x1eT ....
L82: 
L83:     resp.release_conn()
L84: However, you can also treat the cite35†`HTTPResponse` instance as a file-like object. This allows you to do buffering:
L85: 
L86:     import urllib3
L87: 
L88:     resp = urllib3.request(
L89:         "GET",
L90:         "https://httpbin.org/bytes/1024",
L91:         preload_content=False
L92:     )
L93: 
L94:     print(resp.read(4))
L95:     # b"\x88\x1f\x8b\xe5"
L96: Calls to cite36†`read()` will block until more response data is available.
L97: 
L98:     import io
L99:     import urllib3
L100: 
L101:     resp = urllib3.request(
L102:         "GET",
L103:         "https://httpbin.org/bytes/1024",
L104:         preload_content=False
L105:     )
L106: 
L107:     reader = io.BufferedReader(resp, 8)
L108:     print(reader.read(4))
L109:     # b"\xbf\x9c\xd6"
L110: 
L111:     resp.release_conn()
L112: You can use this file-like object to do things like decode the content using cite37†`codecs`†docs.python.org :
L113: 
L114:     import codecs
L115:     import json
L116:     import urllib3
L117: 
L118:     reader = codecs.getreader("utf-8")
L119: 
L120:     resp = urllib3.request(
L121:         "GET",
L122:         "https://httpbin.org/ip",
L123:         preload_content=False
L124:     )
L125: 
L126:     print(json.load(reader(resp)))
L127:     # {"origin": "127.0.0.1"}
L128: 
L129:     resp.release_conn()
L130: ## Proxiescite38†¶ L131: 
L132: You can use cite39†`ProxyManager` to tunnel requests through an HTTP proxy:
L133: 
L134:     import urllib3
L135: 
L136:     proxy = urllib3.ProxyManager("https://localhost:3128/")
L137:     proxy.request("GET", "https://google.com/")
L138: 
L139: 
L140: The usage of cite39†`ProxyManager` is the same as cite27†`PoolManager` .
L141: 
L142: You can connect to a proxy using HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS. urllib3’s behavior will be different depending on the type of proxy you selected and the destination you’re contacting.
L143: ### HTTP and HTTPS Proxiescite40†¶ L144: 
L145: Both HTTP/HTTPS proxies support HTTP and HTTPS destinations. The only difference between them is if you need to establish a TLS connection to the proxy first. You can specify which proxy you need to contact by specifying the proper proxy scheme. (i.e `http://` or `https://`)
L146: 
L147: urllib3’s behavior will be different depending on your proxy and destination:
L148: 
L149:   * HTTP proxy + HTTP destination
L150: 
L151: 
L152: Your request will be forwarded with the cite41†absolute URI†datatracker.ietf.org .
L153:   * HTTP proxy + HTTPS destination
L154: 
L155: 
L156: A TCP tunnel will be established with a cite42†HTTP CONNECT†datatracker.ietf.org . Afterward a TLS connection will be established with the destination and your request will be sent.
L157: 
L158:   * HTTPS proxy + HTTP destination
L159: 
L160: 
L161: A TLS connection will be established to the proxy and later your request will be forwarded with the cite41†absolute URI†datatracker.ietf.org .
L162: 
L163:   * HTTPS proxy + HTTPS destination
L164: A TLS-in-TLS tunnel will be established. An initial TLS connection will be established to the proxy, then an cite42†HTTP CONNECT†datatracker.ietf.org will be sent to establish a TCP connection to the destination and finally a second TLS connection will be established to the destination. You can customize the cite43†`ssl.SSLContext` used for the proxy TLS connection through the `proxy_ssl_context` argument of the cite39†`ProxyManager` class.
L165: For HTTPS proxies we also support forwarding your requests to HTTPS destinations with an cite41†absolute URI†datatracker.ietf.org if the `use_forwarding_for_https` argument is set to `True`. We strongly recommend you only use this option with trusted or corporate proxies as the proxy will have full visibility of your requests.
L166: ### Your proxy appears to only use HTTP and not HTTPScite44†¶ L167: 
L168: If you’re receiving the cite45†`ProxyError` and it mentions your proxy only speaks HTTP and not HTTPS here’s what to do to solve your issue:
L169: 
L170: If you’re using `urllib3` directly, make sure the URL you’re passing into cite39†`urllib3.ProxyManager` starts with `http://` instead of `https://`:
L171: 
L172:     # Do this:
L173:     http = urllib3.ProxyManager("http://...")
L174: 
L175:     # Not this:
L176:     http = urllib3.ProxyManager("https://...")
L177: If instead you’re using `urllib3` through another library like Requests there are multiple ways your proxy could be mis-configured. You need to figure out where the configuration isn’t correct and make the fix there. Some common places to look are environment variables like `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `ALL_PROXY`.
L178: Ensure that the values for all of these environment variables starts with `http://` and not `https://`:
L179: 
L180:     # Check your existing environment variables in bash
L181:     $ env | grep "_PROXY"
L182:     HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8888
L183:     HTTPS_PROXY=https://127.0.0.1:8888  # <--- This setting is the problem!
L184: 
L185:     # Make the fix in your current session and test your script
L186:     $ export HTTPS_PROXY="http://127.0.0.1:8888"
L187:     $ python test-proxy.py  # This should now pass.
L188:     # Persist your change in your shell 'profile' (~/.bashrc, ~/.profile, ~/.bash_profile, etc)
L189:     # You may need to logout and log back in to ensure this works across all programs.
L190:     $ vim ~/.bashrc
L191: If you’re on Windows or macOS your proxy may be getting set at a system level. To check this first ensure that the above environment variables aren’t set then run the following:
L192: 
L193:     $ python -c 'import urllib.request; print(urllib.request.getproxies())'
L194: 
L195: 
L196: If the output of the above command isn’t empty and looks like this:
L197: 
L198:     {
L199:       "http": "http://127.0.0.1:8888",
L200:       "https": "https://127.0.0.1:8888"  # <--- This setting is the problem!
L201:     }
L202: Search how to configure proxies on your operating system and change the `https://...` URL into `http://`. After you make the change the return value of `urllib.request.getproxies()` should be:
L203: 
L204:     {  # Everything is good here! :)
L205:       "http": "http://127.0.0.1:8888",
L206:       "https": "http://127.0.0.1:8888"
L207:     }
L208: 
L209: 
L210: If you still can’t figure out how to configure your proxy after all these steps please cite4†join our community Discord†discord.gg and we’ll try to help you with your issue.
L211: ### SOCKS Proxiescite46†¶ L212: 
L213: For SOCKS, you can use cite47†`SOCKSProxyManager` to connect to SOCKS4 or SOCKS5 proxies. In order to use SOCKS proxies you will need to install cite48†PySocks†pypi.org or install urllib3 with the `socks` extra:
L214: 
L215:     python -m pip install urllib3[socks]
L216: Once PySocks is installed, you can use cite47†`SOCKSProxyManager` :
L217: 
L218:     from urllib3.contrib.socks import SOCKSProxyManager
L219: 
L220:     proxy = SOCKSProxyManager("socks5h://localhost:8889/")
L221:     proxy.request("GET", "https://google.com/")
L222: 
L223: 
L224: Note
L225: 
L226: It is recommended to use `socks5h://` or `socks4a://` schemes in your `proxy_url` to ensure that DNS resolution is done from the remote server instead of client-side when connecting to a domain name.
L227: ## Custom TLS Certificatescite49†¶ L228: Instead of using cite50†certifi†certifi.io you can provide your own certificate authority bundle. This is useful for cases where you’ve generated your own certificates or when you’re using a private certificate authority. Just provide the full path to the certificate bundle when creating a cite27†`PoolManager` :
L229: 
L230:     import urllib3
L231: 
L232:     http = urllib3.PoolManager(
L233:         cert_reqs="CERT_REQUIRED",
L234:         ca_certs="/path/to/your/certificate_bundle"
L235:     )
L236:     resp = http.request("GET", "https://example.com")
L237: When you specify your own certificate bundle only requests that can be verified with that bundle will succeed. It’s recommended to use a separate cite27†`PoolManager` to make requests to URLs that do not need the custom certificate.
L238: ## Custom SNI Hostnamecite51†¶ L239: 
L240: If you want to create a connection to a host over HTTPS which uses SNI, there are two places where the hostname is expected. It must be included in the Host header sent, so that the server will know which host is being requested. The hostname should also match the certificate served by the server, which is checked by urllib3.
L241: Normally, urllib3 takes care of setting and checking these values for you when you connect to a host by name. However, it’s sometimes useful to set a connection’s expected Host header and certificate hostname (subject), especially when you are connecting without using name resolution. For example, you could connect to a server by IP using HTTPS like so:
L242: 
L243:     import urllib3
L244: 
L245:     pool = urllib3.HTTPSConnectionPool(
L246:         "104.154.89.105",
L247:         server_hostname="badssl.com"
L248:     )
L249:     pool.request(
L250:         "GET",
L251:         "/",
L252:         headers={"Host": "badssl.com"},
L253:         assert_same_host=False
L254:     )
